newsitem.title: UK: LPC - NatWest loan plan seen as part of a trend.
newsitem.headline: LPC - NatWest loan plan seen as part of a trend.

text.p: LONDON, Sept 25 (LPC) - National Westminster Bank's plan to securitise $5 billion of corporate loans is part of a broad movement by banks to move marginally profitable assets off balance sheets while retaining strategic relationships with borrowers, bankers say.

Margins on bank loans to large corporate clients are at cyclical lows - with the average AA rated borrower in the UK paying just 13.66 bps over LIBOR - yet banks like NatWest are forced to participate in the sector in order to pave the way for other, more profitable business with borrowers.

To keep the relationship but sell the debt NatWest will have to create an instrument that is attractive to investors while reassuring large corporate borrowers that a securitisation is in their best interests too, observers say.

"How will company treasurers feel about this?" one banker asked. Other banks in London have been working towards increasing the secondary market for corporate loans for much the same reasons. Secondary sales of loans involve selling large chunks of existing loan, usually to sophisticated investors or other banks. Banks are keen to develop these markets because, though some like NatWest can dull the pain of lending at low rates by earning fees for arranging loans and for administrative duties, loans to high-quality borrowers on thin margins are not seen as an ideal use of capital.

But these efforts to foment a secondary market for corporate debt have faced resistance from corporations that are loath to allow their debt to pass outside a small group of relationship banks. That's because secondary sales of debt often carry with them the right to vote on amendments to a loan or participate in negotiations if the borrower goes into default.

NatWest may be able to get around this hurdle by retaining the voting rights itself and selling to investors a stream of interest and repayment of principal in exchange for assuming credit risk. If so, the relationship between the bank and the borrower will be much as before except that the ultimate funding will come from investors.

However, if voting rights are retained by banks an issue for investors is how they would be represented if a loan went bad. NatWest will use high-quality, investment grade loans, thus reducing the likelihood of default, bankers said.
NatWest declined to comment, citing US Securities and Exchange Commission regulations.

Theoretically, securitisation should offer benefits to borrowers if it becomes widespread, bankers say. "It should drive interest rates in the syndicated loan market down because it will add to liquidity," said the head of syndication at a major bank.
This, of course, would only add to banks' motivation to securitise.
